title: So how to solve this?

blocks.text: Redirecting patients who don't need A&E
Discharge: planned dates, targets and escalation thresholds

tips: A specialist team assesses frail older patients as soon as they arrive - Dundee also has 24 dedicated beds.
Nurses, advanced practitioners and geriatricians treat people at home or in their care home, so they don't need to come into hospital.
Therapists, doctors and discharge staff work at weekends too, so patients can be assessed and discharged any day.
Patients can call NHS 24, and a clinician directs them to the right care, sometimes with a booked time at A&E.
People who don't need emergency care are directed to a more suitable service, such as their GP or a pharmacy.
Setting up Power of Attorney in advance avoids a lengthy guardianship process if someone loses capacity while in hospital.
Social workers, discharge coordinators and support workers plan each patient's discharge together.
Patients are given a planned discharge date, with targets and clear actions when delays build up.
Patients go home with temporary care while their longer-term needs are assessed.
More care at home means patients have somewhere to go as soon as they're ready to leave.
Short-term rehab and early reviews of care packages help people regain independence and free up care for others.
When a patient can't make decisions for themselves, Dundee moves quickly to arrange legal authority so they aren't stuck waiting for guardianship.

ending.text: If NHS Scotland reduces A&E waiting times in our 10 shortlisted hospitals they'll solve most of the problem.
Waiting times are the problem but the fix may lie elsewhere - hospital capacity, over 75s and delayed bed days.
